storylines.title: 3 Shields Guarding Every Jar of Honey
storylines.hook: Three shields keep honey from spoiling.
storylines.pitch: Microbes want a feast, but honey has three defenses. Shield 3 is acid. Shield 2 is the bees' hydrogen peroxide, which barely works in ripe honey. Shield 1, the twist, is that honey is so dry it pulls water out of bacteria.
storylines.conflict: Sugary food should be a feast for microbes, yet honey stays safe.
storylines.stakes: Each shield counted down is stronger or stranger than the last, and the peroxide turns out to be nearly switched off.
storylines.twist: The bees' main germ-killer, hydrogen peroxide, is very slow in ripe honey, because that reaction needs water and ripe honey has almost none.
storylines.payoff: The top shield is dryness: honey is hygroscopic, so it dehydrates bacteria, and that is why the jar never spoils.

storylines.title: What If Bacteria Moved Into Your Honey?
storylines.hook: What if bacteria moved into honey?
storylines.pitch: Picture one microbe landing in a jar of honey, ready to settle in. First it meets a sticky, acidic wall. Then honey pulls the water right out of it, and there is too little water left for any microbe to grow. Back in real life, the jar stays fine.
storylines.conflict: A hungry microbe lands in a jar full of sugar and wants to move in.
storylines.stakes: Each step is worse for the microbe: first the acid, then the water being pulled out, then no water left to grow on.
storylines.twist: Honey is hygroscopic, so instead of the microbe taking what it needs, honey draws the moisture out of the microbe.
storylines.payoff: Back to reality: with so little available water, no microorganism can grow, so honey does not spoil.

storylines.title: Honey Suspect Lineup: Who Stops the Germs?
storylines.hook: Which honey trick really stops germs?
storylines.pitch: The host lines up suspects: the bees' hydrogen peroxide, the acid, and the missing water. Our prediction: the peroxide is the star, since it is honey's main antimicrobial agent. The result is a twist: in ripe honey the peroxide is made very slowly, because the reaction needs water and honey has dried from about 70-80% water to about 17-18%.
storylines.conflict: Honey never spoils, but which of its defenses actually does the work?
storylines.stakes: The host puts all the faith in the peroxide, the best-known defender, then finds out it is almost switched off.
storylines.twist: The main antimicrobial agent, hydrogen peroxide, is produced very slowly in mature honey because ripe honey lacks the water the reaction needs.
storylines.payoff: The answer: drying honey down to 17-18% water leaves too little available water for any microbe, with acid as a second barrier.
